abstract.p: The phase 3 COMPASSION-16 trial demonstrates significant progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) benefits with cadonilimab plus standard therapy in patients with persistent, recurrent, or metastatic cervical cancer. This analysis aims to assess efficacy outcomes in patient subgroups of COMPASSION-16. The dual primary endpoints of COMPASSION-16 are PFS, assessed by the blinded independent central review (BICR) according to RECIST version 1.1, and OS. The secondary endpoint is objective response rate. In this subgroup analysis, the PFS, OS and objective response rate are evaluated in subgroups including bevacizumab use, prior concurrent chemoradiotherapy, PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS), metastatic disease at baseline, platinum use, and age. With median follow-up of 25.6 months, hazard ratios (HRs) for PFS favour cadonilimab group in all subgroups. Moreover, the addition of cadonilimab is also associated with prolonged overall survival. This subgroup analysis confirms that improvements in progression-free and overall survival are consistent with the primary results of the COMPASSION-16 study across diverse patient profiles.

The COMPASSION16 trial showed survival benefits of cadonilimab plus standard therapy in advanced cervical cancer. Here, subgroup analysis confirms consistent progression-free and overall survival improvements across diverse patient profiles.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Cervical cancer is the fourth most common neoplasm in females, with approximately 660,000 new cases and 350,000 deaths worldwide in 20221. The standard first-line treatment for persistent, recurrent, or metastatic cervical cancer consists of platinum-based chemotherapy (cisplatin or carboplatin plus paclitaxel), with or without bevacizumab2,3. Nonetheless, the prognosis for these patients remains poor, with an estimated overall survival (OS) of only 13–17 months2. The KEYNOTE-826 trial showed that adding pembrolizumab to the standard treatment improved survival outcomes in patients with a PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS) ≥ 14. However, this regimen did not confer a survival benefit in patients with a PD-L1 CPS < 1.

Cadonilimab is a bispecific antibody that simultaneously binds to PD-1 and CTLA-4. Cadonilimab has shown encouraging antitumor effects in solid tumours both as a monotherapy and in combination with chemotherapy5,6. Notably, cadonilimab monotherapy has been approved as a second-line treatment in recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer by China’s National Medical Products Administration7. Furthermore, the phase 2 COMPASSION-13 trial showed that cadonilimab combined with standard therapy exhibited encouraging antitumor activity with a manageable safety profile in the first-line treatment of recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer, even in those with negative PD-L1 expression8. Recently, the interim analysis results of the phase 3 COMPASSION-16 trial showed that adding cadonilimab to standard chemotherapy with or without bevacizumab significantly improved survival outcomes in patients with persistent, recurrent, or metastatic cervical cancer, and the safety profile was tolerable and manageable9. The median progression-free survival (PFS) was 12.7 months in the cadonilimab group versus 8.1 months in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR] 0.62, 95% CI 0.49-0.80, p < 0.0001); the median OS was not reached versus 22.8 months (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.48–0.86, p = 0.0011)9. The findings suggest that the cadonilimab-based regimen could be an effective and safe first-line treatment option for advanced cervical cancer.

In the preliminary subgroup analysis of COMPASSION-16, all prespecified subgroup analyses showed progression-free survival benefit favouring participants on cadonilimab over placebo. Here, we report the detailed results of the subgroup, including specific median PFS values, subgroup-specific Kaplan-Meier curves, OS values in some specific subgroups and the data of objective response rate in subgroups, to further evaluate the efficacy of this regimen across a range of different patient populations.

sec.title: Patients and treatment
sec.p:
Between September 11, 2021, and June 23, 2022, 445 eligible patients were enroled from 59 clinical sites and randomly assigned to the two treatment groups (222 to the cadonilimab group and 223 to the placebo group) (Fig. 1). All enrolled patients were women. At the data cutoff for the overall survival interim analysis (April 30, 2024), the median follow-up was 25.6 months (IQR 23.6–28.0) in the full analysis set. Baseline characteristics were well balanced between the two groups9. The median age was 56 years (IQR 50–62), and 74 (17%) patients were aged 65 or above. Bevacizumab was administered during the trial in 265 (60%) patients, and 180 (40%) patients did not receive bevacizumab; 215 (48%) patients received prior CCRT, and 230 (52%) did not receive prior CCRT. Regarding PD-L1 expression, 116 (26%) patients had a CPS < 1, 312 (70%) patients had a CPS ≥ 1, and 180 (40%) patients had a CPS ≥ 10. Overall, 323 (73%) had metastatic disease at baseline, and 122 (27%) did not have metastatic disease at baseline; 192 (43%) patients received cisplatin and 253 (57%) received carboplatin.Fig. 1Trial profile.
Source data are provided as a Source Data file.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p:
The median PFS was 15.1 months (95% CI, 11.8, 20.9) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 11.5 months (95% CI, 9.5, 15.5) in the placebo group in patients with bevacizumab use (HR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.57, 1.06); in patients without bevacizumab use, the median PFS was 11.7 months (95% CI, 9.5, 14.7) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 6.7 months (95% CI, 5.6, 7.8) in the placebo group (HR, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.31, 0.63). The Kaplan–Meier curves of PFS by bevacizumab use subgroups and the corresponding forest plot are shown in Fig. 2. The median OS was not reached in both treatment groups in patients with bevacizumab use (HR, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.56, 1.26); in patients without bevacizumab use, the median OS was 28.2 months (95% CI, 17.5, NE) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 15.1 months (95% CI, 12.2, 17.6) in the placebo group (HR, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.33, 0.75).Fig. 2Progression-free survival by bevacizumab use.
Kaplan–Meier estimate in subgroups with bevacizumab use (A) and without bevacizumab use (B), and subgroup analysis (C). Source data are provided as a Source data file.

The median PFS was 16.1 months (95% CI, 11.6, 20.9) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 7.9 months (95% CI, 7.5, 11.5) in the placebo group in the patients with prior CCRT (HR, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.39, 0.78); in those without prior CCRT, the median PFS was 12.0 months (95% CI, 9.7, 14.7) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 8.5 months (95% CI, 7.7, 9.7) in the placebo group (HR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.49, 0.93) (Fig. 3). The median OS was not reached (95% CI, 28.2, NE) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 22.8 months (95% CI, 16.9, NE) in the placebo group in patients with prior CCRT (HR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.35, 0.82); in those without prior CCRT the median OS was 27.0 months (95% CI, 23.2, NE), compared to 24.5 months (95% CI, 15.7, NE) in the placebo group (HR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.52, 1.12).Fig. 3Progression-free survival by prior concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT).
Kaplan–Meier estimate in subgroups with prior CCRT (A) and without prior CCRT (B), and subgroup analysis (C). Source data are provided as a Source data file.

The median PFS was 12.0 months (95% CI, 9.5, 17.1) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 8.2 months (95% CI, 7.8, 11.8) in the placebo group in patients with PD-L1 CPS < 1 (HR, 0.65; 95% CI, 0.42, 1.03); in patients with PD-L1 CPS ≥ 1 the median PFS was 14.7 months (95% CI, 11.4, 19.9) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 8.3 months (95% CI, 7.5, 9.7) in the placebo group (HR, 0.62; 95% CI, 0.47, 0.83); in patients with PD-L1 CPS ≥ 10, the median PFS was 17.1 months (95% CI, 11.4, NE) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 8.1 months (95% CI, 6.9, 11.3) in the placebo group (HR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.37, 0.79) (Fig. 4). The median OS was not reached (95% CI, 23.0, NE) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 25.3 months (95% CI, 17.7, NA) in the placebo group in patients with PD-L1 CPS < 1 (HR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.44, 1.34); in those with PD-L1 CPS ≥ 1, the median OS was not reached (95% CI, 26.6, NE) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 22.7 months (95% CI, 15.5, NE) in the placebo group (HR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.49, 0.97); in those with PD-L1 CPS ≥ 10, the median OS was not reached (95% CI, 26.6, NE) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 29.0 months (95% CI, 16.5, NE) in the placebo group (HR, 0.68; 95% CI, 0.42, 1.08).Fig. 4Progression-free survival by PD-L1 expression.
Kaplan–Meier estimate in subgroups of PD-L1 CPS1 (A), PD-L1 CPS≥1 (B), PD-L1 CPS≥10 (C), and subgroup analysis (D). Source data are provided as a Source data file.

The median PFS was 12.0 months (95% CI, 10.4, 15.1) in the cadonilimab group compared to 8.3 months (95% CI, 7.7, 9.7) in the placebo group in patients who had metastatic disease at baseline (HR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.54, 0.92); in those who did not have metastatic disease at baseline, the median PFS was not reached (95% CI, 11.9, NE), compared to 8.0 months (95% CI, 7.1, 11.7) in the placebo group (HR, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.25, 0.70) (Fig. 5). The median OS was 28.8 months (95% CI, 26.3, NE) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 25.3 months (17.7, NE) in the placebo group in patients who had metastatic disease at baseline (HR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.52, 1.02); in those without metastatic disease at baseline, the median OS was not reached (95% CI, 28.2, NE) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 17.6 months (95% CI, 15.1, 26.4) in the placebo group (HR, 0.48; 95% CI, 0.27, 0.86).Fig. 5Progression-free survival by metastatic disease at baseline.
Kaplan–Meier estimate in subgroups with metastatic disease (A) and without metastatic disease (B), and subgroup analysis (C). Source data are provided as a Source data file.

The median PFS was 14.7 months (95% CI, 11.8, NE) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 8.1 months (95% CI, 7.6, 11.7) in the placebo group in patients who received cisplatin (HR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.34, 0.72); in those who received carboplatin the median PFS was 12.0 months (95%, 9.6, 16.5) in the cadonilimab group, compare to 8.2 months (95% CI, 7.7, 9.7) in the placebo group (HR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.53, 0.97) (Fig. 6). The median OS was not reached (95% CI, NE, NE) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 23.9 months (95% CI, 17.7, NE) in the placebo group in patients who received cisplatin (HR, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.27, 0.70); in those who received carboplatin, the median OS was 27.8 months (95% CI, 20.9, NE) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 22.8 months (95% CI, 15.7, NE) in the placebo group (HR, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.57, 1.18).Fig. 6Progression-free survival by choice of platinum therapy.
Kaplan–Meier estimate in subgroups with cisplatin (A) and with carboplatin (B), and subgroup analysis (C). Source data are provided as a Source data file.

The median PFS was 13.5 months (95% CI, 11.4, 17.3) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 9.5 months (95% CI, 7.8, 10.5) in the placebo group in patients aged <65 years (HR, 0.68; 95% CI, 0.52, 0.88); in those aged ≥65 years, the median PFS was 12.0 months (95% CI, 8.1, NE) in the cadonilimab group, compred to 7.4 months (95% CI, 5.7, 8.4) in the placebo group (HR, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.22, 0.68) (Fig. 7). The median OS was not reached (95% CI, 27.8, NE) in the cadonilimab group, compared to 25.3 months (95% CI, 21.6, NE) in the placebo group in patients aged <65 years (HR, 0.69; 95%, 0.50, 0.95); in those aged ≥65 years, the median OS was 26.6 months (95% CI, 16.5, NE) in the cadonilimab group, compred to 15.1 months (95% CI, 9.6, 17.1) in the placebo group (HR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.27, 0.91).Fig. 7Progression-free survival by age.
Kaplan–Meier estimate in subgroups aged 65 years (A) and ≥65 years (B), and subgroup analysis (C). Source data are provided as a Source data file.

The addition of cadonilimab was associated with higher ORRs across all investigated subgroups. The forest plot of ORR is shown in Fig. 8. ORRs ranged from 74.1% to 87.2% in the cadonilimab group and 51.5% to 78.0% in the placebo group.Fig. 8Subgroup analysis of objective response rate.
Source data are provided as a Source Data file.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Subgroup analyses from the phase 3 COMPASSION-16 study demonstrated that cadonilimab plus chemotherapy with or without bevacizumab had superior overall efficacy compared to the placebo control across all investigated subgroups. The HR values of both PFS and OS were less than 1 in all subgroups. Additionally, the cadonilimab group exhibited higher ORRs across all subgroups. The results reported here complement the primary analyses of the trial, which demonstrated statistically significant improvement in PFS and OS with the addition of cadonilimab9. The reported findings further support that the cadonilimab-based regimen could be an effective treatment for patients with advanced cervical cancer, irrespective of bevacizumab use, previous CCRT, PD-L1 expression, metastatic disease, choice of platinum therapy, and age. This analysis showed a more detailed evaluation of the efficacy of the cadonilimab-based regimen in cervical cancer, providing critical evidence in the treatment of this disease.

First-line treatment options for advanced cervical cancer remain limited. While pembrolizumab plus standard treatment has been approved in patients with PD-L1-positive disease based on the positive results of KETNOTE-8264. However, there is currently no approved immunotherapy for patients with PD-L1-negative advanced cervical cancer. Our subgroup analysis revealed a clear separation of PFS Kaplan–Meier curves in the PD-L1 negative subgroup, suggesting the potential efficacy of the regimen in this patient population. While the OS data were still immature, with the median OS not yet reached, the HR for the median OS was 0.77. We speculate that with longer follow-up, the OS benefit could be observed. Cadonilimab has also shown encouraging efficacy in PD-L1-negative patients in previous clinical trials5,6,8. In patients with positive PD-L1, cadonilimab demonstrated a PFS improvement of 6.4 months (14.7 vs. 8.3 months; HR, 0.62). In the KEYNOTE-826 study, a 2.2-month median PFS improvement (10.4 vs 8.2 months; HR, 0.62) was observed in PD-L1-positive patients4. Furthermore, the PFS benefit with cadonilimab appeared greater in patients with PD-L1 CPS ≥ 10, yielding a 9-month increase (17.1 vs 8.1 months; HR, 0.54). Although cross-trial comparisons should be interpreted with caution, the findings suggest that cadonilimab may confer a survival benefit in advanced cervical cancer, regardless of PD-L1 expression status.

Bevacizumab plays an important role in the treatment of advanced cervical cancer. However, around 40% of cervical cancer patients are ineligible for bevacizumab, and these individuals often experience poorer survival outcomes compared to those who received it4,9. In our study, among patients who did not receive bevacizumab, the addition of cadonilimab improved median PFS by 5 months (11.7 vs 6.7 months; HR, 0.44) with a clear separation of the Kaplan–Meier curves. In contrast, KEYNOTE-826 reported a small 0.1-month improvement (6.3 vs 6.2 months; HR, 0.74) in the same patient subgroup. The efficacy shown in the subgroup without bevacizumab use may be attributable to the combined anti-PD-1 and anti-CTLA-4 activity of cadonilimab10,11. Therefore, cadonilimab presents a potentially effective treatment for patients with contraindications to bevacizumab. The BEATcc trial evaluated atezolizumab plus standard treatment in bevacizumab-eligible patients12. In the subgroup of patients eligible for bevacizumab, our subgroup analysis results were similar to the results of BEATcc and the subgroup analysis findings from the KEYNOTE-826 study12,13.

The phase 3 trial JCOG0505 established that carboplatin-paclitaxel was non-inferior to cisplatin-paclitaxel for metastatic or recurrent cervical cancer14. In our trial, the addition of cadonilimab improved median PFS in both the cisplatin (14.7 vs 8.1 months; HR, 0.49) and the carboplatin subgroup (12.0 vs 8.2 months; HR, 0.72). The improvement seemed to be more evident in the cisplatin subgroup, which was consistent with the subgroup analyses from KEYNOTE-82613.

The addition of cadonilimab demonstrated improvement in median PFS in those who received prior CCRT (16.1 vs 7.9 months; HR, 0.55) and those who did not (12.0 vs 8.5 months; HR, 0.67). The treatment effect seemed to be more pronounced in those with prior CCRT. Furthermore, patients without metastatic disease at baseline had a greater improvement in survival with cadonilimab compared to those without metastatic disease at baseline. Finally, the subgroup analyses demonstrated that the addition of cadonilimab improved survival outcomes in advanced cervical cancer patients regardless of their age. Women ≥65 years are more likely to present with advanced cervical cancer at diagnosis compared to younger women15. However, older cervical cancer patients are frequently undertreated, which contributes to a higher mortality16,17. In our subgroup analysis, the addition of cadonilimab prolonged PFS by 4.6 months and OS by 11.1 months in those aged ≥65 years. Cadonilimab plus standard treatment presents a safe and feasible option for women in this older age group.

The main limitation of this study lies in the nature of subgroup analyses. Unlike in the primary analyses populations, the subgroup analyses were not powered to demonstrate differences between treatment arms in the subgroups. Caution is needed when interpreting the findings, particularly in smaller subgroups with a limited number of events. In conclusion, subgroup analyses of the phase 3 COMPASSION-16 study showed that the addition of cadonilimab improved PFS and OS across various demographic and clinical subgroups, consistent with results for the overall population. These findings support the use of cadonilimab plus chemotherapy with or without bevacizumab as a standard of care for patients with diverse clinical characteristics who have persistent, recurrent, or metastatic cervical cancer.

sec.title: Study design and patients
sec.p: The study protocol and all amendments were approved by the institutional review board or ethics committee of the leading study site (Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Centre) and other study sites. The names of all ethics committees and approval numbers have been published9. All patients provided written informed consent before participating in the study.

The COMPASSION-16 study was a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter phase 3 trial conducted in 59 clinical sites in China. This trial assessed the efficacy and safety of cadonilimab (10 mg/kg) or placebo in combination chemotherapy (cisplatin [50 mg/m2] or carboplatin [area under the curve 4-5] plus paclitaxel [175 mg/m2]), with or without bevacizumab (15 mg/kg). Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio by the study investigator. Participants, investigators, clinical staff, the study sponsor, and the data analysts were masked to treatment assignment. The regimen was administered every 3 weeks for six cycles, followed by cadonilimab or placebo with or without bevacizumab every 3 weeks as maintenance therapy. Treatment was continued until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, no further clinical benefit as determined by the investigator, withdrawal of consent, or having received cadonilimab or placebo for 2 years. Eligible patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio and stratified by the use of bevacizumab (yes or no) and previous concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT; yes or no). Randomisation was performed centrally through an interactive web-response system. The investigator would decide the use of cisplatin or carboplatin and bevacizumab before randomisation. The placebo was administered in the same manner as cadonilimab during the treatment period. Investigators, patients and other participants were unaware of the treatment assignment of patients.

Eligible patients had previously untreated persistent, recurrent, or metastatic (stage IVB) cervical cancer of squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, or adenosquamous carcinoma, not amenable to curative surgery or CCRT; had at least one measurable tumour lesion according to Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours (RECIST) version 1.1; had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1; and had adequate organ function. CCRT for curative intent or as a neoadjuvant or adjuvant treatment within 90 days before randomisation, or previous treatment targeting the mechanism of tumour immunity (e.g., anti-angiogenic therapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors, or therapy against immune costimulatory factors) were not permitted. All enrolled patients were female. Information on the sex of all enrolled participants was collected based on self-reporting by the patients. All patients were recruited at hospital centres participating in this study in China, and all enrolled patients were Chinese patients. The full eligibility criteria were available in the study protocol9.

sec.title: Endpoints and assessments
sec.p: The dual primary endpoints of the trial were PFS, assessed by the blinded independent central review (BICR) according to RECIST version 1.1, and OS. The objective response rate (ORR) defined as the proportion of patients with either complete response or partial response according to RECIST version 1.1 by investigator was a secondary endpoint. Tumour imaging was performed at screening, every 6 weeks for the first 24 weeks, every 9 weeks from week 25 to week 51, and every 12 weeks thereafter until disease progression, initiation of new antitumor therapy, death, or study closure, whichever occurred first. Survival outcomes continued to be collected every 3 months after the last dose. PD-L1 expression in tumour tissues was assessed by immunohistochemistry using Monoclonal Mouse Anti-Human PD-L1 Clone 22C3 (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA) at the central laboratory, and measured by CPS, defined as the number of PD-L1-positive cells (tumour cells, lymphocytes, and macrophages) divided by the total number of tumour cells multiplied by 100.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The pre-specified subgroups used for this analysis included concomitant bevacizumab use or not, prior CCRT or not, PD-L1 CPS (<1, ≥1, or ≥10), metastatic disease at baseline or not, choice of carboplatin or cisplatin, and aged <65 years or ≥65 years. There is no formal hypothesis testing in this subgroup analysis. Efficacy analyses of PFS and OS were assessed in the full analysis set, which included all randomly assigned patients. The median PFS and OS and their corresponding 95% CIs were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method. The HRs and their corresponding 95% CIs for the subgroups were estimated from an unstratified Cox proportional hazards model. The Clopper–Pearson method was used to calculate the 95% CIs for the ORR of each treatment group. Data collection was performed using Medidata EDC. All statistical analysis were done using SAS version 9.4.
